common_name: Black Beauty Mulberry (Large Sweet Black Mulberry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Black Beauty is self-fertile and does not require a pollinator, and it fruits at a young age.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; established trees are drought-tolerant. Black Beauty is a black mulberry selection prized for producing unusually large, elongated berries with the rich, intensely sweet-tart, wine-like flavor characteristic of true black mulberry (Morus nigra), widely regarded among mulberry enthusiasts as having the finest flavor of any mulberry species — deeper, more complex, and more balanced between sweet and tart than the milder white or red mulberries. The large fruit size makes hand harvest more efficient than picking the smaller berries of many other mulberry types. Because ripe mulberries drop as they mature and stain heavily, plant away from patios, walkways, and parking areas, or spread a sheet beneath the canopy at harvest time to catch fruit. Trees need only light annual pruning to maintain shape and size.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Mulberry Varieties

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Unryu is grown primarily as an ornamental specimen for its dramatically twisted, contorted branch structure, which is especially striking in winter when leafless.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Unryu, meaning 'dragon's claw' in Japanese, is an ornamental white mulberry selection grown chiefly for its strikingly twisted, corkscrew-contorted branches, a dramatic sculptural feature that is most visible and prized in winter after leaf drop, and which also makes the cut branches valued by florists and flower arrangers. It produces small, sweet, mild-flavored white-to-pinkish mulberries in season, a secondary bonus to its main ornamental appeal. Because the twisted branch character can be lost in overly vigorous growth, avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization, and prune minimally, removing only dead or crossing wood, to preserve the natural contorted form. Like other mulberries, ripe fruit drops and stains, so site it away from paved areas.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown plants in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Issai is self-fertile, precocious, and compact, often fruiting the first year after planting and staying small enough for a large container.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, or grow in a large container where its compact, naturally dwarf habit is a real advantage. Issai is a Japanese-bred mulberry selection prized for its exceptional precocity — plants commonly bear their first crop within a year of planting, far faster than seedling or standard-sized mulberry cultivars — combined with a compact, easily managed size well suited to small yards, espalier training, and container culture. The sweet, juicy, dark purple-black berries ripen over an extended season, and the plant is self-fertile, needing no second tree for pollination. Because of its smaller stature, Issai is easier to net against birds and to harvest by hand than full-sized mulberry trees, while still producing a generous crop relative to its size. Prune to control height and encourage branching if a bushier form is desired.
sources: One Green World Nursery — Mulberry Cultivar Notes
California Rare Fruit Growers — Mulberry Varieties
